sentences.text: Texasetes was an armored dinosaur belonging to the group Ankylosauria, reaching about 3 meters in length and 1.2 meters in height.
Scientists estimate its weight at 550 kilograms, identifying it as a compact, small quadrupedal herbivore.
Its body was protected by osteoderms on the back and limbs, supported by a horizontally oriented ilium and ankylosaurian shoulder morphology.
The holotype specimen USNM 337987 consists of a skull fragment, two teeth, various vertebrae, partial limbs, and several osteoderms.
Coombs speculated that the individual died on the shore or in a river, was flushed to sea, decomposed, and lost elements like distal limbs before burial.
The genus was recovered from the Paw Paw Formation near Haslet, Tarrant County, Texas, a site that also yielded the nodosaurid Pawpawsaurus.
The genus Texasetes was named by Coombs in 1995.
Texasetes belongs to the dinosaur class Ornithischia and is classified within the family Nodosauridae, with the type species Texasetes pleurohalio.
While Coombs assigned the specimen to the family Nodosauridae, Vickaryous et al. consider it an Ankylosauria of uncertain placement.
Texasetes lived approximately 100 million years ago during the Albian stage of the Middle Cretaceous, specifically from 106.3 to 100.5 million years ago.
It is debated whether Pawpawsaurus is synonymous with Texasetes; while they share age and formation, Arbour et al. (2016) found Pawpawsaurus closer to Europelta and Texasetes closer to Edmontonia.
Vickaryous et al. consider the phylogenetic position of Texasetes to be Ankylosauria incertae sedis, reflecting uncertainty about its exact family placement.
A 2016 analysis determined that a juvenile ankylosaurian skeleton from the Paw Paw Formation was more closely related to Niobrarasaurus than to either Pawpawsaurus or Texasetes.
